items.followUp: Define a cofactor and give one example of a co-enzyme.

rubric.why: A co-enzyme is an organic, non-protein substance that assists an enzyme.
rubric.description: Defines a co-enzyme as an organic, non-protein substance associated with enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an organic substance, not a protein, that assists an enzyme.

rubric.why: A correct example completes the answer.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a co-enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example, such as NAD, FAD or co-enzyme A.

modelAnswer: A co-enzyme is an organic substance, not a protein, that associates with an enzyme and helps it carry out a reaction.
Examples include NAD, FAD and co-enzyme A.

items.followUp: State two ways in which roots are adapted for absorbing water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: Root hairs are extensions or outgrowths of root epidermal cells.
rubric.description: Defines root hairs as extensions or outgrowths of root epidermal cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying root hairs as extensions or outgrowths of root epidermal cells.

rubric.why: Root hairs absorb water and mineral salts and increase the root's absorptive surface area.
rubric.description: States a function of root hairs: absorbing water and mineral salts, or increasing surface area for absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the absorption function or the increase in absorptive surface area.

modelAnswer: Root hairs are thin extensions of the epidermal cells of a root.
They absorb water and mineral salts from the soil and increase the root's surface area for absorption.

items.followUp: Name two proteins found in blood plasma and state one function of either.

rubric.why: Albumins and globulins are important proteins in blood plasma.
rubric.description: Names albumins and globulins as plasma proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both albumins and globulins.

rubric.why: Fibrinogen is another important protein present in blood plasma.
rubric.description: Names fibrinogen as a plasma protein.

modelAnswer: Important proteins present in blood plasma include albumins, globulins and fibrinogen.

items.followUp: Explain the tissue level and organ-system level of organization, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: An organ consists of different tissues working together to perform a function.
rubric.description: Defines an organ as different tissues working together for a specific function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that an organ is made of different tissues working together.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the organ level.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an organ.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an appropriate organ example, such as stomach, heart, leaf or kidney.

rubric.why: An organ system consists of organs working together to perform related functions.
rubric.description: Defines an organ system as a group of organs working together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that organs work together in an organ system.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the organ-system level.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an organ system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an appropriate organ-system example.

modelAnswer: An organ is a structure made of different tissues working together to perform a specific function; for example, the stomach.
An organ system is a group of organs working together to perform related functions; for example, the digestive system.

items.followUp: State the main rules for writing the scientific name of an organism, using humans as an example.

rubric.why: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a scientific name consisting of two words.
rubric.description: Defines binomial nomenclature as a system of giving organisms two-word scientific names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the scientific name consists of two words.

rubric.why: The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
rubric.description: States that the genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this naming rule.

rubric.why: The second word is the species name and begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.description: States that the species name comes second and begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this naming rule.

rubric.why: Scientific names are italicized in print or underlined when handwritten.
rubric.description: States the formatting rule for scientific names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that names are italicized in print or underlined when handwritten.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a scientific name consisting of two words.
The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
The second word is the species name and begins with a lowercase letter.
The two words are italicized in print; when handwritten, they are underlined separately.
